chunks: Bus contention causes and cures. The question: What is bus contention?
Bus contention means two or more outputs are driving the same wire at the same time, to different levels.
One is pushing the wire up to the supply while another pulls it down to ground. That makes a direct path from supply to ground through both outputs.
The result is a wire stuck at a mid-level that reads as garbage, a large wasted current, and hot or damaged output circuits.
Imagine a tug of war over a marker on a rope. One team pulls the marker toward the high end. The other team pulls it toward the low end.
If the teams are equally strong, the marker stays in the middle and neither team wins. But both teams strain hard the whole time, which is wasted effort that tires them out.
Here the strain is current, and the tiring is heat.
Equivalent circuit of two push-pull drivers in contention. A's on PMOS is R on P to the supply, B's on NMOS is R on N to ground. The shared wire is the divider tap.
Nothing in the circuit limits the current except those two small resistors.
Contention: two outputs driving one wire to opposite levels at once. On-resistance: the small resistance, tens of ohms, that an output's switch has when it is on.
It is all that limits the current in a fight. Tri-state (high impedance): an output that can switch off completely, so another device may drive the wire.
Open-drain: an output that can only pull low, so it cannot fight.
Two pins on a 3. 3 volts board each have about 25 ohms of on-resistance. One drives high and one drives low. The current is 3.
3 over (25 plus 25) equals 66 milliamps, well above a typical pin's rating. The wire sits at the midpoint, 1. 65 volts.
A receiver treats below 30% of the supply as low and above 70% as high, so 1. 65 volts is neither.
A 100 ohms resistor in series with each pin cuts the current to about 13 milliamps. That is the whole idea.
"Bus contention is two drivers actively driving the same wire to opposite levels.
With push-pull outputs that's a path from supply to ground through two on-resistances: with 25 ohms each at 3. 3 volts, about 66 milliamps, and the wire sits near 1.
65 volts, an invalid logic level, while the output stages get hot.
It happens with two masters, software bugs, a device that won't release the bus, or overlapping enables on a bidirectional bus.
Avoid it with tri-state drivers and dead time, open-drain with a pull-up for shared lines, chip selects, series resistors and safe reset states."
